characters: Delali: an 11-year-old girl with short natural hair, a white school blouse and navy skirt, always with a pencil behind her ear.
Togbe Kwami: Delali’s grandfather, an elderly maize farmer in a straw hat and a faded checked shirt.
Selorm: Delali’s classmate, 11, in a green polo shirt, with a plastic-bottle gauge of his own.
Madam Rukaya: the class teacher, in a lilac dress and glasses, who prepares the bottles and leaves the rest to the class.

teacherGuide.overview: A data-collection story where students do the measuring, find a flaw in their own set-up and report honestly. It respects a farmer’s knowledge while showing why numbers help.
learningGoals: Say what a week of data can and cannot show.
beforeReading: Ask learners how they know whether it has rained a lot or a little.
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to add the numbers themselves.
At page 5, ask for reasons why the readings might differ.
afterReading: Make a class rain gauge and record for at least two weeks.
discussion: What can one week of data not tell us?
reflection: What question about the weather could you answer with your own measurements?

mathsExtension.task: What was the average rainfall per day, to one decimal place?
If 1 mm of rain is 1 litre per square metre, how many litres fell on a 200-square-metre field in the week?

support: Provide a pre-drawn table and a ready-made gauge.
stretch: Compare a gauge in the open with one under a tree for a fortnight and describe the difference.

culturalNotes: Rainfall is vital to farming in Ghana; farmers’ own observations are valuable alongside measurements. Delali, Selorm and Togbe Kwami are verified Ewe names/titles (Togbe means Grandfather in Ewe).
localiseThis: Check your local rainy season dates; the story does not claim the rains were really late.
An adult should cut the bottles.

investigation.title: Make a rain gauge
materials: A clear plastic bottle with straight sides (teacher-cut)
steps: An adult cuts the top off the bottle.
Turn the top upside down inside the bottle as a funnel.
Add a little water to level the base and tape the ruler so zero lines up with the water level.
Place the gauge in an open space and read it at the same time each day.
Empty it after reading and record in a table.
investigation.whatToNotice: Do readings differ if the gauge is moved? What changes the numbers?
investigation.safetyNote: An adult must cut the plastic. Do not go outside during thunderstorms.

factCheck.claim: 1 mm of rainfall equals 1 litre of water per square metre.
factCheck.explanation: A depth of 1 mm over 1 square metre is 0.001 cubic metres, which is 1 litre.
factCheck.reference: National meteorological services and the World Meteorological Organization (confirm the exact page before publishing)

reviewerNotes: Confirm open vowel (ɔ) without rhotic r.
